GOODWILL OF A PROFESSIONAL PRACTICE OR BUSINESS IN A MARITAL DISSOLUTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET AND THE PARTIES IT CONCERNS
This Professional Practice Goodwill Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, whose marital dissolution or legal separation proceeding is pending, or may be filed, in the California superior court for Sacramento County, and in which one asset that may be in question is described as a solo dental practice in Sacramento. It describes what California statutes and published California appellate decisions say about “goodwill” as a divisible item of the community estate: how California statutes define the goodwill of a business, when the goodwill of a professional practice has been treated as a community asset, what a court is required to do when a professional practice is part of the community estate, what valuation approaches the published decisions have approved or rejected, the rule that no valuation method may rest on a spouse's post-marital efforts or continuing income, the holding that goodwill exists only in connection with a business rather than in a natural person's skill and reputation, when a valuation date other than the time of trial may be used, and how an asset that cannot be physically divided may be awarded to one spouse. This information sheet states what those authorities say in general terms. It does not determine whether any practice or business of Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee has goodwill, whether any goodwill is community property or separate property, what any goodwill is worth, what valuation method fits any particular practice, or how any community estate should be divided; those are matters for the court to decide on the specific facts and the evidence presented.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION: GOODWILL IS THE EXPECTATION OF CONTINUED PUBLIC PATRONAGE, AND IT IS PROPERTY
California's definition of goodwill does not appear in the Family Code. It appears in the Business and Professions Code, in a chapter titled “Good Will.” Section 14100 states that the good will of a business is the expectation of continued public patronage. Section 14102 states that the good will of a business is property and is transferable. Both sections were added by the Legislature in 1941 and carry forward language traceable to the 1872 Civil Code. Published California decisions dividing the goodwill of a professional practice in a dissolution proceeding have taken these two sections as their starting point: section 14100 supplies what goodwill is, and section 14102 supplies the characteristic — that it is property — which is what allows goodwill to be an item of the community estate a court divides.

A 1969 DECISION HELD THE GOODWILL OF A SOLE PRACTITIONER'S PROFESSIONAL PRACTICE IS TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT IN DIVIDING THE COMMUNITY
In Golden v. Golden (1969) 270 Cal.App.2d 401, a physician appealed from a divorce decree in which the trial court had valued the community assets to include an allocation of $32,500 for the good will of his practice, awarded that good will to him, and required him to pay his wife her half in cash and monthly installments. He argued the trial court erred in finding the good will of his practice to be a community asset, relying on a decision holding that on the dissolution of a law partnership no allowance could be made for good will because the firm's reputation depended on the skill of each member. The Court of Appeal rejected that analogy. It reasoned that when a partnership is dissolved a court cannot say which partner will carry the firm's good will away, but that in a matrimonial matter the sole practitioner's practice continues with the same intangible value it had during the marriage, and that under community property principles the other spouse contributed to that value just as to any other earnings and accumulations during marriage. The judgment was affirmed.

FOSTER: THE VALUE MUST EXIST AT DISSOLUTION AND CANNOT DEPEND ON THE PRACTITIONER'S CONTINUING INCOME, AND NO RIGID VALUATION RULE APPLIES
In In re Marriage of Foster (1974) 42 Cal.App.3d 577, the Court of Appeal reviewed a $27,000 valuation of the goodwill of a physician's medical practice. The parties there conceded that the practice had goodwill, so the appeal turned on the method of valuation and the sufficiency of the evidence. The court stated two limits that later decisions have repeated. First, because a community interest can be acquired only during the marriage, the value of the goodwill must exist at the time of the dissolution, and that value must be established without dependence on the potential or continuing net income of the professional spouse. Second, the court stated that no rigid and unvarying rules govern the determination of goodwill value; each case turns on its own facts and circumstances, and the evidence must be such as legitimately establishes value. The court added that when goodwill attaches to a business its value is a question of fact, that opinion evidence is admissible but not conclusive, and that the trier of fact may consider such things as the situation of the business premises, the amount of patronage, the personality of the persons engaged in the business, how long the business has been established, and the habit of customers in continuing to patronize it.

FOSTER: COMMUNITY GOODWILL IS NOT LIMITED TO WHAT A WILLING BUYER WOULD PAY, AND NO METHOD MAY COUNT POST-MARITAL EFFORTS
The Foster court also addressed an earlier decision, In re Marriage of Fortier (1973) 34 Cal.App.3d 384, which had described the value of community goodwill as the market value at which the goodwill could be sold upon dissolution. Foster declined to read Fortier as restricting valuation to market value. It stated that the value of community goodwill is not necessarily the specified amount of money a willing buyer would pay, observing that in view of the exigencies ordinarily attendant on a marriage dissolution the amount obtainable in the marketplace might well be less than the true value, and that community goodwill is a portion of the community value of the professional practice as a going concern on the date of dissolution. The court then summarized the rule it drew from these principles: goodwill may not be valued by any method that takes into account the post-marital efforts of either spouse, but any legitimate method that measures present value by taking into account some past result is permissible, and for this purpose the practice is assumed to continue in the future. Applying that rule, the court affirmed the $27,000 figure, because the expert's method had used past earnings projected into present value rather than the practitioner's future efforts or future earnings.

A 1985 DECISION: THE COURT MUST DETERMINE WHETHER GOODWILL EXISTS, AND AN UNSALABLE PRACTICE IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY WITHOUT GOODWILL
In In re Marriage of Watts (1985) 171 Cal.App.3d 366, the trial court had found that a surgeon's medical practice had no goodwill. Two experts had reached that conclusion using a market-value or comparable-sales approach, reasoning that no market existed for the practice; the other spouse's expert, using a capitalized excess-earnings approach, had valued the goodwill at $293,000. The Court of Appeal stated that in a dissolution case involving a professional practice the court must determine whether goodwill exists and, if it does, must value it and take it into consideration in dividing the community property. Reviewing the findings, the court held the trial court erred, because its own specific findings on the practitioner's earnings and on what a comparable surgeon could earn implied excess earnings that conflicted with its finding of none. The court further stated that it would have been error to find no goodwill simply because there was no market for the practice, and concluded that the mere fact a professional practice cannot be sold will not, standing alone, justify a finding that the practice has no goodwill or that the community goodwill has no value. The matter was remanded for a determination in accordance with the opinion.

MCTIERNAN & DUBROW: DIVISIBLE GOODWILL ATTACHES TO A BUSINESS, NOT TO A PERSON'S SKILL AND REPUTATION
In In re Marriage of McTiernan & Dubrow (2005) 133 Cal.App.4th 1090, the trial court had found that a motion picture director possessed goodwill worth $1.5 million, based on his “elite professional standing” and a quantifiable expectation of continued patronage, and had valued it by the excess-earnings method. The Court of Appeal held that finding erroneous. It reasoned that although the expectation of continued public patronage is one aspect of goodwill under Business and Professions Code section 14100, section 14102 also makes the goodwill of a business property that is transferable, so the controlling question was what “a business” means. The court held that the term refers to a professional, commercial or industrial enterprise with assets rather than to a natural person, resting on the historical understanding of goodwill as an incident of a going concern, on the unamended 1872-derived text of the two sections, and on the requirement that what is divided be property. Applying that reading, the court held that the ability to perform the excess-earnings calculation did not convert the director's skill and reputation into a business or transmute his talents into transferable property, and that the trial court had erred in finding goodwill in his practice or career as a motion picture director. The judgment was ordered modified to delete the $1.5 million from the assets subject to division.

HOW THE EXCESS-EARNINGS METHOD HAS BEEN DESCRIBED BY A COURT OF APPEAL
The excess-earnings method recurs throughout the published California goodwill decisions reported in this document. In In re Marriage of Garrity & Bishton (1986) 181 Cal.App.3d 675, the Court of Appeal set out the steps of that method in a footnote. As described there, one first determines the practitioner's average annual net earnings before income taxes, using any period that seems reasonably illustrative of the current rate of earnings; one then determines the annual salary of a typical salaried employee whose experience is commensurate with the practitioner's; one deducts from the average net pretax earnings of the practice a fair return on the net tangible assets the business uses; one subtracts the comparable salary figure from what remains, yielding the “excess earnings”; and one capitalizes those excess earnings by multiplying them by a factor equal to a period of years, discounted to present value, with the period varying according to such factors as the type of business, its stability, and its earnings trend.

GARRITY & BISHTON: VALUING THE PRACTICE REQUIRES MORE THAN A GOODWILL CALCULATION
Garrity & Bishton also addressed what happens when a court values an entire professional practice by running the goodwill calculation alone. Both spouses there were lawyers. The trial court, having stated that the excess-earnings method was the most appropriate method for valuing the good will and practice of each party, found that each law practice had no value at all. The Court of Appeal held that was error. It pointed to In re Marriage of Lopez (1974) 38 Cal.App.3d 93, which listed the assets and liabilities a court should examine in valuing a law practice — fixed assets such as cash, furniture, equipment, supplies and the law library; other assets such as properly aged accounts receivable, costs advanced with due regard for collectability, and work in progress or completed but not billed; the goodwill of the practitioner in the law business as a going concern; and the liabilities of the practitioner related to the business. The court stated that this approach provides a realistic measure of a practice's actual value and that the method the trial court used failed to take those items into account. Because the two spouses' practices were interwoven in the judgment, the court reversed the zero valuations of both.

ROSEN: A FLAWED EXCESS-EARNINGS ANALYSIS CAN LEAVE A PRACTICE WITH A GOODWILL VALUE OF ZERO
In In re Marriage of Rosen (2002) 105 Cal.App.4th 808, the trial court found that a sole practitioner's law practice had a goodwill value based on excess earnings of roughly $42,000 per year. The Court of Appeal held the finding erroneous. The expert had used a single year's net income rather than an average, and conceded that averaging over any period of years would have produced nominal or no excess earnings and hence little or no goodwill value; the trial court had also used average gross cash flow where the method calls for net income. The court stated that the excess-earnings method is not the only measure of goodwill value and that goodwill may be measured by any legitimate method that measures present value by taking into account some past result, so long as the evidence legitimately establishes value — but that the expert's analysis did not legitimately establish value under the excess-earnings method and that he offered no opinion under any other method. It directed that on remand the law practice be assigned a goodwill value of zero in the final distribution.

ACKERMAN: GOODWILL VALUE IS A QUESTION OF FACT REVIEWED FOR SUBSTANTIAL EVIDENCE, AND CAPITALIZED EXCESS EARNINGS IS A RECOGNIZED TECHNIQUE
In In re Marriage of Ackerman (2006) 146 Cal.App.4th 191, a spouse challenged the trial court's calculation of the goodwill of a plastic surgery practice. The Court of Appeal restated the governing standards and affirmed on this point. expectedJSON.body: In In re Marriage of Rosen (2002) 105 Cal.App.4th 808, the trial court found that a sole practitioner's law practice had a goodwill value based on excess earnings of roughly $42,000 per year. The Court of Appeal held the finding erroneous. The expert had used a single year's net income rather than an average, and conceded that averaging over any period of years would have produced nominal or no excess earnings and hence little or no goodwill value; the trial court had also used average gross cash flow where the method calls for net income. The court stated that the excess-earnings method is not the only measure of goodwill value and that goodwill may be measured by any legitimate method that measures present value by taking into account some past result, so long as the evidence legitimately establishes value — but that the expert's analysis did not legitimately establish value under the excess-earnings method and that he offered no opinion under any other method. It directed that on remand the law practice be assigned a goodwill value of zero in the final distribution.

expectedJSON.body: Family Code section 2552 supplies the timing rule that a goodwill valuation must satisfy. Subdivision (a) states that, for the purpose of dividing the community estate on dissolution or legal separation, and except as provided in subdivision (b), the court shall value the assets and liabilities as near as practicable to the time of trial. Subdivision (b) supplies the exception: on 30 days' notice by the moving party to the other party, the court may for good cause shown value all or any portion of the assets and liabilities at a date after separation and before trial, in order to accomplish an equal division of the community estate in an equitable manner. This timing rule operates alongside the case law reported elsewhere in this document, under which the value of community goodwill must not depend on the post-marital efforts or the continuing income of the professional spouse.

expectedJSON.body: Two Family Code sections explain why a goodwill figure has practical consequences. Section 2550 states that, except on the parties' written agreement or an oral stipulation in open court, or as otherwise provided in the division, the court in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding shall divide the community estate of the parties equally, whether in the judgment or later if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to do so. Because the goodwill of a practice cannot be split in kind between two people, section 2601 supplies the mechanism courts use: where economic circumstances warrant, the court may award an asset of the community estate to one party, on such conditions as the court deems proper, to effect a substantially equal division of the community estate. In the reported goodwill cases the practice and its goodwill are awarded to the practitioner spouse, and the value assigned to that goodwill drives the offsetting cash or property the other spouse receives.
